extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and fans seeking an overview of Australian comedy and its characteristics
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey of Australian comedy: its characteristic tone, historical origins, major forms (stage, radio, TV, film, stand-up, songs, cartoons), notable practitioners, festivals and awards, and cultural influences such as multiculturalism and larrikinism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian sense of humour (tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: The "Australian sense of humour" is often characterised as dry, irreverent and ironic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include performers Barry Humphries and Paul Hogan and character creations such as Norman Gunston and Roy and HG; expressed across film, literature and media. This criterion signals the expected tonal register for material considered typically Australian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larrikinism and anti-authoritarianism
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaudeville larrikinism and an irreverent, anti-authoritarian streak are hallmarks of Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically traced to convict origins and ANZAC dark humour; manifested in performers like Graham Kennedy and in self-mocking portrayals of national stereotypes. Works that emphasise cheeky, roguish, or anti-establishment attitudes fit this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-mockery and parochial satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-mockery and parochial (local) satire are central strains in Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen in sitcoms like Kath & Kim, films such as The Castle, and TV parodies like Roy and HG. Effective Australian comedy often pokes fun at Australian society, accents, suburban life and national obsessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Australian slang and vernacular
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of Australian slang and vernacular language gives comedy a distinctly Australian flavour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples include the work of Henry Lawson, Banjo Paterson, comic songs and vaudeville catchphrases; novelty songs and character dialogue often rely on local idioms to create humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multicultural and migrant influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiculturalism contributes to diversity in Australian comedy through migrant and ethnic perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mary Coustas, Anh Do, Nick Giannopoulos and parody forms (Guido Hatzis). Comedy that engages immigrant experiences, cultural clashes or ethnic stereotypes (often satirically) exemplifies this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indigenous and Aboriginal contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aboriginal performers and perspectives form part of the national comedic tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ernie Dingo is highlighted as an example. Inclusion of Indigenous voices and stories is a distinctive strand within Australian comedy practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character creation and impersonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Invented comic characters and impersonations are a major form (e.g., Barry Humphries' Dame Edna, Sir Les Patterson; impersonators like Gerry Connolly, Max Gillies, Billy Birmingham).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character work is used to satirise social vices, snobbery and celebrity culture; success often depends on sharpening national traits and performing them to both local and international audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdist, dadaist and deadpan styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdist/dadaist and deadpan delivery are notable stylistic approaches in Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barry Humphries' dadaist humour, Elliot Goblet's deadpan stand-up and other performers exemplify this. Material that trades on surreal or understated delivery falls under this rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bawdy and risque strands
rubrics_metrics.description: A bawdy, ribald strain exists alongside more genteel or cerebral comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers like Rodney Rude and Austen Tayshus represent bawdy comedy; novelty singles and rude observational bits fit this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical and novelty-song comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic songs and musical novelty have been important, from vaudeville and country-comedy to chart hits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Chad Morgan, Slim Dusty ('Pub With No Beer'), John Williamson ('Old Man Emu') and comedic singles like The Twelfth Man's parodies; lyrics often use mock-profundity and local references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film themes: self-mockery, outback vs urban contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Australian cinema often employs self-mockery and contrasts between outback stereotypes and urban life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited films: Crocodile Dundee (fish-out-of-water), The Castle (suburban satire), Strictly Ballroom, The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert. Successful films often trade on recognisable national images and affectionate critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television tradition: sketch dominance and vaudeville roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch comedy (more than sitcom formula) has been a popular and enduring form on Australian TV, growing out of vaudeville talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows cited: The Mavis Bramston Show, The Naked Vicar Show, The Paul Hogan Show, The D-Generation, Fast Forward, Full Frontal, The Late Show, The Comedy Company. Television also features talk-show wit and mockumentary styles (Chris Lilley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political satire and current-affairs lampooning
rubrics_metrics.description: Cynical political satire and lampooning of media and politics is an enduring strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include The Chaser's War on Everything, Frontline, The Hollowmen, Rubbery Figures, John Clarke & Bryan Dawe. Material that skewers politicians, institutions and media practices qualifies here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand-up ecosystem and festival importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up is a major contemporary form supported by a nationwide circuit and festivals, notably the Melbourne International Comedy Festival (MICF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stand-up appears in venues from pubs to major auditoria; MICF and Raw Comedy (emerging-comedian competition) are central institutions. Festival success and circuit visibility are measures of stand-up prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio and duo formats as outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio programmes and comedy duos have provided significant platform and reach for Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable radio acts: Roy & HG, Merrick and Rosso, Martin/Molloy, Hamish & Andy. Radio format influences comedic pacing and recurring characters/segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartoons and political cartooning
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoons — including long-running strips and political cartoons — are integral to Australian satirical tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: The Bulletin magazine cartoons, Will Dyson, Ginger Meggs; contemporary cartoonists like Michael Leunig. Cartoons serve as concise social and political commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition through awards and festivals
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal recognition and culture-building are signalled by festivals and awards (MICF, Sydney/Brisbane festivals, Raw Comedy Award, Logie categories, Australian Film Institute awards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Festival presence, awards and televised finals are indicators of success and mainstream acceptance; the Bald Archy parody prize is an example of satirical institutional culture.
